# Interactive Text-to-SQL Generation via Editable Step-by-Step Explanations

## Research question

Users may recognize a wrong result but lack a precise, understandable way to locate and repair the corresponding SQL component.

## Method

STEPS explains SQL clause by clause using grammar rules, then converts edited explanations into query updates. Aligned entity edits use direct transformation; larger changes use a SmBoP-based text-to-clause model trained on 83,000 generated explanation–clause pairs. Composition heuristics add joins, merge clauses and discard duplicate ordering/grouping clauses.

## Evaluation

Reference-aware simulation on Spider, Spider-DK, Spider-Syn and WikiSQL supplies corrected gold-clause explanations. A separate counterbalanced study recruits 24 participants to complete eight Spider tasks per tool in ten minutes using STEPS, MISP or a DIY reimplementation. Metrics include exact-set/execution matching, completed and correct tasks, skips and subjective confidence/load.

## What the results support

Simulation reaches 97.9% exact-set match with EditSQL. Real users average 5.7 correct of eight assigned tasks, with 85.81% correctness among completed tasks. The hybrid correction method matches the neural-only accuracy at lower reported correction latency; direct transformation alone has narrower coverage.

## Limits and qualifications

Simulation assumes perfect error localization and correction, unlike real users. The human sample is small, tutorial durations differ, and skipped/unattempted tasks are outside its accuracy denominator. NL-EDIT comparison numbers are imported, not rerun. Some listed paraphrases alter equality boundaries. Support is limited to Spider query constructs; clarification decisions, abstention and context-dependent multi-question dialogues are not evaluated.

## Relevance to reliable Text-to-SQL

An adjacent human-feedback mechanism that makes the location and content of corrections explicit, useful for studying verification effort without conflating oracle feedback with realistic interaction.

## Checks against the paper

These are interpretations checked against the source, not verbatim quotations attributed to its authors.

| Claim or inference examined | Original evidence | Location | Assessment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The 97.9% result demonstrates near-perfect performance with ordinary users. | Section 4.1 compares predicted and reference clauses, then deletes erroneous steps or supplies paraphrased explanations derived from the correct clauses. Section 9 explicitly calls this optimistic and not representative of real-world use. Table 1 reports the resulting 97.9% exact-set match. | Sections 4.1–4.3, PDF pages 5–6; Table 1, page 6; Section 9, page 10 | Report a reference-aware simulation result. It tests repair given idealized feedback, not autonomous error detection, natural clarification or real-user success. |
| Real users solve 85.81% of all assigned tasks. | Section 5.4 defines task completion accuracy as correct divided by completed. Table 5 reports 6.7 completed and 5.7 correct tasks from eight assigned, with 0.3 skipped. Sessions last ten minutes; tutorial videos last six minutes for STEPS, three for MISP and two for DIY. | Sections 5.3–5.4 and Table 5, PDF page 8 | Preserve the completed-task denominator and report the correct-task count alongside it. Do not interpret accuracy or subjective confidence as guaranteed intent correctness. |
| The paper establishes a controlled, matched-feedback superiority over NL-EDIT. | The authors could not run NL-EDIT because of missing code and runtime problems and instead use its published accuracy. STEPS simulation supplies corrected explanations of gold clauses, whereas the original NL-EDIT task consumes recorded user feedback. | Footnote 1, PDF page 2; Sections 4.1–4.3, pages 5–6; existing NL-EDIT primary task description | Treat the numerical comparison as protocol-dependent rather than a fresh matched-feedback reproduction. NL-EDIT was not included in the real-user study. |
| The synthetic paraphrasing rules necessarily preserve the SQL meaning. | Appendix B/Table 9 permits greater than to become no less than and less than to become no more than. Those substitutions change whether equality is included. The same alternatives appear in the pinned Paraphrase/replacement_dict.json source. | Appendix B, PDF page 13; Table 9, page 15; pinned Paraphrase/replacement_dict.json greater than and less than entries | A concrete semantic-quality caveat for the rule inventory; the number of affected generated examples and any impact on reported scores were not measured. |
| Editable explanations support arbitrary SQL and evaluated conversational ambiguity resolution. | Section 9 limits the implementation to keywords appearing in Spider and excludes update operations. It also states that evaluation concerns single-turn SQL generation; context-dependent multi-turn extension is future work. Component matching is used as an evaluation heuristic, not a general equivalence proof. | Sections 4.1 and 9, PDF pages 5 and 10; Appendix A, pages 13–14 | Describe iterative repair of an initial query within the supported grammar, without claiming complete ambiguity coverage, refusal handling or preservation guarantees. |
